Before pursuing tests for gastrinoma (fasting gastrin, secretin stimulation), I need the result of the noninvasive H. pylori test I ordered — a positive result would make H. pylori-associated duodenal ulcers the single most likely diagnosis; a negative result would prompt evaluation for acid hypersecretion. The key initial diagnostic test is a fasting serum gastrin level (with gastric pH if possible) to detect inappropriate hypergastrinemia; an elevated fasting gastrin with low gastric pH supports gastrinoma and would prompt a secretin stimulation test. I'll order a fasting serum gastrin.

5. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy findings: Multiple duodenal ulcers
3. Calcium 13.2 mg/dL (elevated)
13. Palpation: Mild epigastric tenderness

Fasting serum gastrin level: Normal
Gastric pH / fasting gastric acid status: Normal

[THOUGHT] Multiple duodenal ulcers in a young patient with negative H. pylori and no NSAID use strongly point to acid hypersecretion from a gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome). The marked hypercalcemia suggests concomitant primary hyperparathyroidism — raising concern for MEN1, where gastrinomas can be intermittent and fasting gastrin may be normal at a single timepoint. Overall, the combination of multiple DU ulcers plus hypercalcemia makes Zollinger–Ellison syndrome the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma), likely MEN1-associated.
